hint: the social radar — reading a room and sensing what people feel or need without being told. Closest: 'tact'/'social awareness', but 눈치 is a skill you are openly judged on. 눈치가 빠르다 = quick to read; 눈치가 없다 = oblivious; 눈치를 보다 = to watch someone's mood warily

情 — the attachment that accumulates between people (or toward places, even objects) through shared time. NOT romantic love; it is why Koreans stay in relationships logic says to leave. 정이 들다 = to grow attached, 정이 많다 = warm-hearted
'our' used where English says 'my' — 우리 엄마, 우리 집, 우리 나라, even 우리 남편. Marks belonging to a shared group rather than possession. Saying 제 엄마 sounds cold and odd to Korean ears
loyalty owed to people who stood by you — standing by them in turn, even at a cost. Closest: 'loyalty', but 의리 carries moral obligation. Also used jokingly: 의리 없다! = you traitor
being in someone's debt for their help. 신세를 지다 = to impose on someone's kindness. Koreans track this carefully and repay it; English has no single word for the discomfort of owing
to look after someone's needs before being asked — packing their lunch, remembering their medicine, checking they ate. Closest: 'take care of', but 챙기다 is about noticing first and acting
warm and attentive in how one speaks and treats you; affectionate without being sappy. Said of someone who makes you feel looked after
brusque and undemonstrative, showing no warmth on the surface — but not unkind. The classic description of a Korean father
to be shy and stiff around people one doesn't know yet. One word for a whole behavior; English needs 'to be shy with strangers'. Also said of babies
for 정 to form — to grow attached to a person, a place, even an old phone, through time spent together
恨 — accumulated, unresolved grief and resentment carried over a lifetime or a nation's history; sorrow hardened into endurance. Considered a core Korean sentiment, invoked for 판소리 and for history
chest-tight frustration at something that won't move — a slow explanation, a blocked plan, stuffy air, a person who won't get it. One word covers all of them
the anguish of being wrongly blamed, or punished past what is fair. English 'unfair' describes the situation; 억울하다 describes what it does to you inside
mild regret that something good ended too soon or fell just short. Not sad — wistful. Used constantly: 벌써 가? 아쉽다
quietly hurt that someone close didn't do as much as you'd hoped. NOT anger, NOT betrayal — it stings precisely because you care. The hardest Korean feeling word for English speakers
the fluttery anticipation before something you're looking forward to. Closest: 'excited', but 설레다 is the physical flutter itself, and the standard word for early romance
the warm swelling in the chest when proud of what you or someone close achieved. Quieter and warmer than 'proud'
relieved and sad at once — exactly the feeling of a graduation, a last day at work, a long project ending. Two opposite feelings fused into one word
to sulk over a small slight and show it, expecting to be coaxed back. Affectionate when said of friends or couples
a tender ache of pity — watching an aging parent work hard, or a kid trying too hard. Closest: 'heartbreaking', but softer and more loving
heartsore — upset in a way that gnaws at you, over something gone wrong or someone you care about. Literally 'the insides hurt'

火病 — physical illness brought on by anger and grief suppressed for years. Recognized in Korean medicine and once listed in the DSM as a culture-bound syndrome; classically ascribed to women of an older generation

'refreshing' — but Koreans say it of ice water AND scalding soup, of a massage that hurts, and of a problem finally resolved. It means RELIEF, not temperature. The most misunderstood word on this list
the clean, light feeling after a shower, a good sleep, or finally settling something that had been hanging over you
heavy and greasy in a way that coats the mouth — cream, cheese, fried food. ALSO used of a person who is cheesy and over-smooth
the nutty, toasty savouriness of sesame oil, roasted seeds, perilla. ALSO means quiet satisfaction when someone who wronged you gets what they deserve — one word, two unrelated senses
clean and light on the palate, not rich or heavily seasoned — a compliment for food. Also said of a person's plain, unpretentious manner
deliberately cute, endearing behaviour deployed to charm — a voice, a gesture, a pout. A social skill rather than mere cuteness. 애교 부리다 = to act cute on purpose
babyish, clingy acting-up toward someone who dotes on you, to get attention or a favour. 어리광 부리다
shamelessly playing innocent while knowing exactly what you're doing, keeping a straight face throughout
uninvited meddling in other people's business. 오지랖이 넓다 = literally 'your coat lapel is wide' = you butt into everything
immature for one's age, not yet grown into sense. The opposite, 철들다, means to finally come of age emotionally — a milestone Koreans name explicitly
subtly, more than you'd expect or admit. 은근히 맛있어 = 'it's surprisingly good, actually'. Softens a compliment or a complaint
forcing yourself, or being forced, to do something against your will. 억지로 먹다 = to eat when you don't want to
roughly, good-enough, without full effort. Can be practical (대충 훑어봤어 = I skimmed it) or a criticism. Extremely common in daily speech
abuse of power by whoever holds the stronger position — a client toward a vendor, a boss toward staff. From 갑 = 'party A' in a contract. Drives Korean news cycles
the after-work team dinner, usually with drinking. Officially team bonding, often effectively compulsory — a defining feature of Korean work life
'an eye-stamp' — showing your face so that the person who matters registers you were there. 눈도장 찍다 = to make sure you're seen
reacting to news everyone else processed long ago. 뒷북치다 = to be late to the party, said with teasing
so hectic there's no headspace left — frazzled, all over the place. Used of a day, a room, or a person
to put in effort — but mainly used as a parting greeting. 수고하셨습니다 = 'thank you for your work today', said when leaving or to someone ending a shift. English has no farewell like it
'as you see fit', 'on your own judgment'. 알아서 해 can mean a warm 'do it however you like' or a cold 'figure it out yourself' — tone decides which
talking about someone behind their back after the fact. 뒷담화 까다 = to badmouth a person who isn't there
to treat everyone because something good happened to YOU — a raise, a new job, good news. The one with the fortune pays, not the guests
'rice strength' — the belief that stamina and resilience come from eating properly. 밥심으로 산다 = you live on the power of your meals
being the same age as someone. In Korea this instantly settles speech level and closeness, so it's among the first things people establish on meeting
a housewarming where you invite people to your new home; guests traditionally bring detergent or toilet paper (wishes for things to flow and bubble up)
eating specific restorative foods (삼계탕 and the like) to rebuild the body's strength, especially in midsummer. Health as maintenance rather than treatment
exaggerating how hurt or tired you are to get sympathy. 엄살 부리다 = to play it up. Affectionate or dismissive depending on tone
open-handed generosity, especially giving a little extra unasked. 인심이 좋다 = generous; the market vendor's 덤 is 인심 in action
